analysis.one_liner: Bars members of Congress and their families from personally trading stocks by requiring their investments be placed in blind trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 80 cosponsors from both parties, never got a hearing or a vote in the House Committee on House Administration and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every member of Congress, along with their spouse and dependent children, to place stocks, commodities, and similar investments into a blind trust — meaning someone else manages the money and the lawmaker does not know what is being bought or sold. Investments could stay in the trust until 180 days after the member leaves office, and members would have to publicly certify compliance. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain confidence that lawmakers cannot use private knowledge of upcoming legislation, regulation, or hearings to profit in the stock market. Members' families would also be spared pressure to trade on inside information.

how_it_helps.text: Requires members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children to put covered investments — stocks, commodities, futures, and derivatives — into a qualified blind trust managed by someone else.
Members must certify compliance to the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate, and those certifications are posted on public websites.
Trusts cannot be dissolved, and assets cannot be controlled, until 180 days after the member leaves office.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children, who would lose direct control of their stock and commodity investments for their entire tenure plus 180 days, and would bear the administrative cost of setting up blind trusts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: Members and their families would lose hands-on control of their investments for the rest of the member's tenure plus 180 days, and must pay to establish and manage a qualified blind trust.
Blind trusts are not perfect: a member may still know roughly what assets they hold, so the arrangement reduces but cannot fully eliminate potential conflicts of interest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a direct fix to a well-documented conflict of interest: lawmakers trading stocks while shaping the rules that move markets. The cost is that members and their families would give up hands-on control of investments and pay trust-management fees, and some argue blind trusts are imperfect at blocking all inside knowledge. Weighed against the size of the conflict being removed, the costs are modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House committee that handles such bills and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 12, 2023 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee reporting the bill or the House voting on it.
The bill attracted 80 cosponsors, including 18 Republicans and 62 Democrats, and its original sponsors included members of both parties such as Chip Roy (R) and Emanuel Cleaver (D).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families keep the ability to personally trade stocks in sectors their own committee work affects; no one else gains.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who keep trading rights

against.name: House Committee on House Administration leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over member-trading rules
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it stalled in committee.

against.name: House leadership of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 62 of 216 Democrats and 18 of 224 Republicans cosponsored — but neither party's leadership moved the bill out of committee.

industries.industry: Securities and financial services industry (relative to member-trading volumes)
industries.note: Any trading by members and their families would flow through blind trusts rather than self-directed accounts, though the overall market impact would be negligible.
The bill would restrict a personal financial privilege of sitting lawmakers, which is why the affected parties are also the ones who decide whether it advances.
